questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Function on Which to Apply a Root-Finding Method When Applying the Trapezoidal Method
questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}=6\sqrt{x}\,{y}^{2},\,y(1)=2
$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx=1,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **general form** of $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ in terms of the new values ${x}_{\text{new}}$ and ${y}_{\text{new}},$ and the current values $x$ and $y?$
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(6\sqrt{x}\,{y}^{2}+6\sqrt{{x}_{\text{new}}}\,{y}_{\text{new}}^{2})\cdot 1 \\  & =3\sqrt{x}\,{y}^{2}+3\sqrt{{x}_{\text{new}}}\,{y}_{\text{new}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+3\sqrt{x}\,{y}^{2}+3\sqrt{{x}_{\text{new}}}\,{y}_{\text{new}}^{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{{{y}_{\text{new}}-3\sqrt{{x}_{\text{new}}}\,{y}_{\text{new}}^{2}-y-3\sqrt{x}\,{y}^{2}}_{⏟}}_{g({y}_{\text{new}})}=0.
$$

Therefore, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-3\sqrt{{x}_{\text{new}}}\,{y}_{\text{new}}^{2}-y-3\sqrt{x}\,{y}^{2}.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}\sqrt{y},\,y(1)=1
$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx=1,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **specific function** $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ used in the first step?
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}\sqrt{y}+({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}})\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}+\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{2}({x}_{\text{new}})^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-y-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2}\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-1-\frac{1}{2}(1)^{2}\sqrt{1} \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}-2\sqrt{{y}_{\text{new}}}-\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}-y,\,y(1)=1
$$

Using the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx=1,$ the new value ${y}_{\text{new}}$ is obtained by solving the equation $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0$ at each step. Which of the following is the **specific function** $g({y}_{\text{new}})$ used in the first step?
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

In this example  $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(({x}^{2}-y)+({x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}))\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}),\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}-y-\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}})=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})={y}_{\text{new}}-y-\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-y+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}).
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

Therefore, the function used in the first step is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & ={y}_{\text{new}}-1-\frac{1}{2}({1}^{2}-1+{2}^{2}-{y}_{\text{new}}) \\  & ={y}_{\text{new}}-1-\frac{1}{2}(0+4-{y}_{\text{new}}) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{y}_{\text{new}}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}+{y}^{3},\,y(1)=-1.4
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(2).$ Round your answer to two decimal places.

$y(2)≈$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=2-1=1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general, $Δy$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(({x}^{2}+{y}^{3})+({x}_{\text{new}}^{2}+({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}))\cdot 1 \\  & =0.5{x}^{2}+0.5{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}+0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{\text{new}} & =y+Δy \\ {y}_{\text{new}} & =y+0.5{x}^{2}+0.5{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}+0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3},\end{aligned}
$$

and moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+0.5{x}^{2}+0.5{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}+y-{y}_{\text{new}}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+0.5{x}^{2}+0.5{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}+y-{y}_{\text{new}}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

 Then, the function $g$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+0.5(1)^{2}+0.5(-1.4)^{3}+0.5(2)^{2}-1.4-{y}_{\text{new}} \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+0.5-1.372+2-1.4-{y}_{\text{new}} \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}-{y}_{\text{new}}-0.272.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=-1.4$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}.
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=1.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}-1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{3}-({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-0.272}{1.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}-1}.
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(1)=-1.4,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =-1.4 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & ≈-1.274\,227 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈-1.251\,778 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈-1.251\,069\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈-1.25,$ rounded to two decimal places.

questions.problem:
Consider the following initial value problem:

$$
{y}^{′}={x}^{2}-{y}^{3},\,y(1)=1
$$

Use the trapezoidal method with one step and Newton's method to approximate $y(2).$ Round your answer to two decimal places.

$y(2)≈$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
For an initial value problem

$$
{y}^{′}=f(x,y),\,y(a)=c,
$$

the trapezoidal method with step size $Δx$ is given by

$$
Δy=\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\,Δx,
$$

with ${y}_{\text{new}}^{′}=f({x}_{\text{new}},{y}_{\text{new}})$ evaluated at the next $x$ and $y$ values.

Since we want to find the value of $y$ at $x=2,$ we will use a step size of

$$
Δx=2-1=1.
$$

Now, let's proceed with the trapezoidal method. In general,

$$
\begin{aligned}Δy & =\frac{1}{2}({y}^{′}+{y}_{\text{new}}^{′})\cdot Δx \\  & =\frac{1}{2}({x}^{2}-{y}^{3}+{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-({y}_{\text{new}})^{3})\cdot 1 \\  & =0.5{x}^{2}-0.5{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into ${y}_{\text{new}}=y+Δy,$ we obtain

$$
{y}_{\text{new}}=y+0.5{x}^{2}-0.5{y}^{3}+0.5{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}.
$$

Moving all terms to the left-hand side gives the equation

$$
0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5{y}^{3}-y-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-0.5{x}^{2}=0.
$$

So, the general form of the function $g$ for step size $Δx=1$ is

$$
g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5{y}^{3}-y-0.5{x}_{\text{new}}^{2}-0.5{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, in the first step, the new $x$ value is

$$
{x}_{\text{new}}=x+Δx=1+1=2.
$$

 Then the function $g$ becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}g({y}_{\text{new}}) & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}+0.5(1)^{3}-1-0.5\cdot {2}^{2}-0.5\cdot {1}^{2} \\  & =0.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{3}+{y}_{\text{new}}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

We use a root-finding method with starting point $y=1$ to solve $g({y}_{\text{new}})=0.$ We'll use Newton's method:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{g({y}_{\text{new}})}{{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})}.
$$

Note that the derivative of $g$ is

$$
{g}^{′}({y}_{\text{new}})=1.5({y}_{\text{new}})^{2}+1.
$$

Therefore, our Newton's method iterative scheme is as follows:

$$
({y}_{\text{new}})_{n+1}=({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-\frac{0.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{3}+({y}_{\text{new}})_{n}-3}{1.5(({y}_{\text{new}})_{n})^{2}+1}.
$$

Applying several iterations of Newton's method starting with $y(1)=1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}({y}_{\text{new}})_{1} & =1 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{2} & ≈1.600\,00 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{3} & ≈1.466\,116 \\ ({y}_{\text{new}})_{4} & ≈1.456\,216\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that $y(2)≈1.46,$ rounded to two decimal places.
